[SINGAPORE] The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has issued new guidelines spelling out supervisory expectations for financial institutions to manage risks arising from artificial intelligence use. The Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management will take effect on Oct 7, 2027, and apply to all financial institutions and all forms of AI technologies. The central bank noted in a media statement on Wednesday (Oct 7) that financial regulators and international bodies are “highlighting the need to manage AI risks effectively while enabling firms to realise the benefits of adoption”. The guidelines follow a public consultation, where respondents expressed “strong support” for a principles-based and risk-proportionate approach, said MAS. Meanwhile, financial institutions should assess how to best meet these expectations based on the nature and scale of their AI use, it added. GoCardless has processed what it describes as the UK's first live agentic bank payment, a recurring charity donation set up from start to finish by an AI agent operating under Financial Conduct Authority supervision. The payment, a monthly gift to the anti-poverty charity Trussell , was completed inside a conversational checkout: an AI agent answered questions about the charity's work, presented monthly giving options of £5, £10 or £15, then set up a Direct Debit mandate once the donor chose an amount. It is an early production test of account-to-account rails as the infrastructure for agentic commerce, the emerging model in which AI agents buy and pay on a customer's behalf within limits the customer sets. The demonstration is small in monetary terms, but the timing is deliberate. GoCardless, now a Mollie company following the completion of a roughly €1. 05bn acquisition on 1 September 2026, is trying to establish bank payments rather than cards as the default rail for AI-driven purchases before the category scales. What actually happened in the transaction?. The entire interaction took place within an AI chat rather than a conventional web form. A donor could ask about Trussell, review how each donation tier would be used, and confirm a monthly commitment, at which point the agent prompted for bank details and created the Direct Debit mandate. GoCardless says the flow was designed so the payer keeps control at every step, reflecting its own consumer research in which 64% of UK adults surveyed said they were open to AI managing recurring payments provided they retained control over limits or final approval. That figure is a company-stated survey result rather than an independent finding. Why is GoCardless backing Direct Debit for agentic payments?. The strategic argument is about fit. Direct Debit and recurring open banking payments are built around standing consent and repeat collection, which maps onto the kind of recurring, rules-based spending that consumers appear most willing to delegate to an agent. Cards, by contrast, were designed for one-off authorisation. GoCardless has argued for some time that account-to-account payments are the natural foundation for agentic commerce, and this transaction is intended to convert that positioning into a working reference case. That framing sits against a specific commercial backdrop. GoCardless reported £126. 8m in revenue for its 2024 financial year, up 38% year on year, and recorded its first EBITDA-positive quarter in summer 2025 before the Mollie deal closed. An early lead in agentic account-to-account payments would give the combined group, which serves more than 350,000 businesses across 30-plus markets, a point of difference against card-centric competitors. How big could agentic commerce actually become?. The prize is significant but still speculative. Morgan Stanley Research estimated in December 2025 that agentic shoppers could account for between $190bn and $385bn of US e-commerce spending by 2030, equivalent to 10% to 20% of the online retail market. The $385bn figure GoCardless cites is the top, bull-case end of that range rather than a central estimate, a distinction worth holding onto given how early adoption remains. Most of the agentic-commerce infrastructure announced by large networks and processors to date has been built around cards, which makes an account-to-account entrant a notable counterpoint rather than the consensus approach. GoCardless built the checkout inside the FCA's AI Live Testing programme, a supervised scheme launched in 2025 that lets firms trial consumer-facing AI in live markets with regulatory and technical oversight. Banks and credit unions must therefore redefine where their employees create value. The Trusted Advisor Role Must Evolve. The title “trusted financial advisor” has traditionally suggested that a banker understands a customer’s needs, recommends suitable products, provides guidance, and builds a lasting relationship. In practice, most financial institutions have not provided employees with the training, tools, or time needed to deliver that full experience consistently. It is unrealistic to expect one banker to remember every detail of each relationship, track every product update, understand every financial topic, and provide comprehensive advice during a limited interaction. Generative AI can help solve part of that challenge by making relevant information, analysis, and institutional knowledge easier to access. This does not make human employees less important. It changes how institutions should design customer service and define the banker’s role. Two Strategic Paths for Financial Institutions. Bank and credit union leaders should consider two broad approaches. The first is to continue with a traditional service model. The second is to equip employees with approved generative AI tools so they can provide faster, more informed, and more personalized support. Generative AI is already reducing the value of some work bankers perform today. Everyday AI tools can analyze transactions, identify patterns, summarize financial information, and suggest possible next steps quickly. New Delhi [India], October 6 (ANI): India should focus on expanding the use of existing artificial intelligence applications across the economy and selectively invest in frontier AI capabilities instead of making broad investments in developing advanced models from scratch, Vincent Belinga, Senior Economist at the World Bank, told ANI in an exclusive conversation. Belinga said India should follow a three-stage approach to AI development: adoption, adaptation and frontier development. "One is adoption, meaning using existing application. The second is adaptation, meaning taking open source AI and adapting them to local conditions. And then the third stage is frontier model, meaning developing the next capability from scratch," Belinga said. He said India's immediate priority should be to deepen AI adoption among firms and workers, as adoption is increasing but remains limited across the economy. "What we recommend for India is doing the two. Meaning, deepening adoption so that many firms, millions of firms, millions of workers use AI more productively because so far we see that adoption is increasing but not broad based," he said. Belinga said India already has promising AI applications in areas such as education and healthcare, but many of these initiatives are either limited to specific states or remain at the project stage. The focus, he said, should be on taking such applications to a larger population. "Some promising small AI in education, in health that are either state specific or that are still at project level. So, what we need is to scale up these initiatives so that they are broadly shared across all the states or enriching the broader population," he said. "AI is going to raise productivity," he said, adding that India needs to ensure that AI is adopted across sectors and by workers. It also estimates that AI could add 0. 1-0. 8 percentage points to annual labour productivity growth over the next decade, depending on the pace of AI deployment and complementary investments. title: State Regulators Enter AI Chat: CSBS Releases AI Supervisory Framework
excerpt: The Conference of State Bank Supervisors (CSBS) released an AI Supervisory Framework to help state examiners assess artificial intelligence (AI) use by state-chartered banks and state-licensed nonbank financial institutions. Although the framework is discretionary and creates no new legal obligations, it signals what examiners may expect of an institution’s AI program as institutions increasingly integrate AI into their operations. Background. CSBS supports the nationwide network of state financial regulators, who collectively supervise the substantial majority of state-chartered banks and a range of nonbank financial services providers – including money transmitters, consumer and mortgage lenders and servicers, and debt collectors. CSBS established an AI Advisory Group in August 2024, demonstrating an interest in the development and use of AI in the financial services industry. The AI Supervisory Framework, approved in August 2026, builds on that initiative and fills a regulatory guidance gap left by federal banking agencies. CSBS President and CEO Brandon Milhorn described the framework as “a principles-based approach to governance intended to help financial institutions explore and implement [generative and agentic] AI with additional confidence. ” Importantly, each state agency may independently decide how much, if any, of the framework to incorporate into its own exam program. However, because it offers a common set of questions and procedures that any examiner can adopt, entities operating across multiple states can likely expect meaningful consistency in how AI use and integration in financial institutions will be examined. Overview of the framework. CSBS released the framework in five components built on established resources, including NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework and generative AI profile, the Cyber Risk Institute’s Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework, the US Treasury’s AI Lexicon, and existing prudential guidance (SR 23-4 on third-party risk and SR 26-2 on model risk):. Core examiner guide. This foundation of the framework sets out:. An eight-question initial scoping questionnaire for examiners to use during examinations – covering, among other things, customer-facing AI use, reliance on third parties for AI use and handling of sensitive data with respect to AI processing. A document request list to provide to examinees. Procedures that examiners may use to evaluate an entity’s governance and oversight, AI inventory and use cases, and use of generative AI and other emerging forms and uses of AI. Examiner work program. This 28-page companion document expands each scoping question and procedure with additional guidance, source citations and specific areas of supervisory focus, and provides guidance on how examiners should evaluate agentic AI systems’ permission boundaries, human checkpoints, logging, reversibility and capability to halt actions when needed. Nonbank AI supplements. These supplements serve as overlays that apply AI-specific considerations to three existing nonbank review areas:. Third-party and vendor oversight. Model risk management. Consumer protection. CSBS notes a single AI use case may implicate more than one supplement. AI use case risk tiering worksheet. This optional, institution-completed tool assigns each AI use case a risk tier from 1 (lowest) to 3 (highest) based on consumer impact, human oversight, potential harm from errors or outages, and data sensitivity. Expected controls escalate by tier – from maintaining basic inventories and acceptable-use policies for Tier 1 use cases to independent model validation and AI-specific incident response procedures for Tier 3 use cases. Speaking at a discussion moderated by CNN’s Fareed Zakaria at Columbia University, Banga highlighted the potential of what he called “small AI” — predictive tools designed to improve productivity in areas such as agriculture, education, skilling and healthcare. As an example, he pointed to an AI initiative launched in Uttar Pradesh in collaboration with Google, which is helping women farmers identify crop diseases using basic mobile phones. Banga said the programme connects women farmers associated with cooperatives to an application that does not require advanced technical skills. A farmer can speak into a 3G phone and use its camera to photograph a diseased plant leaf. The application can then identify the disease and recommend a suitable insecticide available through the local cooperative. Instead, he said developing countries could benefit more immediately from smaller, targeted AI applications that address specific problems. “What's really an opportunity there is what we call small AI, which is predictive tools used to improve the productivity of farmer, of better education and skilling, or of improved capabilities in healthcare,” Banga said. title: New RATHat Android Malware Uses Artificial Intelligence to Target Banking Apps
excerpt: . SHARE. A newly identified Android malware strain known as RATHat can take extensive control of infected smartphones by exploiting native accessibility features and leveraging artificial intelligence to manipulate applications and compromise banking data. According to technical assessments conducted by cybersecurity researchers at Cleafy and Zimperium, the threat automates malicious actions directly on compromised handsets without requiring victims to attach their devices to a computer or use a physical cable. By fusing privileged system permissions with automated decision-making tools, the malicious program poses an immediate hazard to financial accounts, authentication information, and stored credentials. ​ Abuse of accessibility services enables shell-level access. ​The initial phase of an intrusion depends on persuading the smartphone user to grant accessibility permissions, a subsystem originally developed within the Android operating system to assist individuals with disabilities. When hijacked by malicious software, these extensive privileges grant visibility across the entire interface, allowing the application to observe on-screen content, locate visual elements, and execute user inputs without manual participation. ​RATHat broadens this attack chain by deploying its accessibility control to autonomously switch on Android wireless debugging. By activating this developer configuration directly on the handset, the malware secures a shell-level foothold in the underlying environment. This elevated standing significantly magnifies the scope of subsequent actions, giving attackers the freedom to bypass standard operational limits, monitor installed programs, and extract sensitive financial data. ​ Artificial intelligence aids automated application navigation. ​A defining characteristic highlighted by the researchers is the software’s use of artificial intelligence to interpret interface elements on the fly. Rather than adhering to fixed coordinate maps or rigid sequential commands that can easily break during software revisions, the integrated AI module analyzes visual layouts in real time. This mechanism helps the program recognize specific buttons, input fields, and navigational cues across varied mobile interfaces. ​This flexibility represents an operational advantage against standard financial applications, which frequently change their layouts, visual structures, and underlying defense measures. Because traditional automation tools typically fail when an interface shifts, the AI-driven approach allows the malware to adapt its actions dynamically. As a result, the tool can continue interacting with financial portals, monitoring authentication data, and siphoning account details even after target platforms issue interface updates. ​ Heightened risks highlight user vigilance and permission control. ​The emergence of RATHat highlights a broader transformation across the mobile threat landscape, where criminal software moves past passive data theft toward direct, automated control of targeted devices. Because the malware can orchestrate complete attack sequences in the background, fraudulent activity becomes considerably more difficult for ordinary consumers to detect while their handsets are in use. ​Security specialists emphasize that avoiding unverified software sources and scrutinizing permission prompts remains critical to defending mobile devices. Users are advised to exercise extreme caution whenever applications request accessibility access without a clear operational purpose. In addition, keeping developer options and wireless debugging protocols turned off helps prevent untrusted software from converting standard mobile permissions into persistent administrative control. Frequently that level of coordination is missing. Processing Content. Only 28% of the 1,500 executives surveyed by IBM report a joint road map with IT backed by a shared cadence. Seventy-three percent say they struggle to coordinate consistently across the C-suite. The IBM Institute for Business Value study , released Sept. 21, draws on two surveys conducted with Oxford Economic from April through June 2026. The respondents are across 21 geographics and 23 industries and not limited to U. S. banks. They raise a relevant question nonetheless. As AI moves into business processes, who should participate in the adoption effort, and what should each participant contribute?. Set direction from the top. In the early days of adoption, AI initiatives often begin with individuals who see an opportunity to improve their work. Developing that idea into a capability requires broader commitments. Funding, data access, changes to responsibilities and decisions about acceptable risk may involve multiple departments, each with its own priorities. Senior leadership is positioned to resolve those trade-offs and hold the organization to a shared objective. My research in 2019 identified leadership vision alongside cost, talent, technology and time as major hurdles to adoption. Case studies in that report also emphasized AI's ability to augment human judgement. The organizational implications became more explicit in my 2021 report , which identified senior management support, an organization-wide strategy and proper organizational structure as foundations for systematic adoption. These reports feature more than a dozen case studies, each accompanied by a detailed AI organizational analysis specific to the respective initiative. For a bank, making a full commitment to AI means specifying the business outcomes AI should help achieve and giving the people responsible the resources and authority to pursue them. Die vietnamesische Staatsbank hat kürzlich das Rundschreiben Nr. 53/2026/TT-NHNN zur Regelung von Sicherheit, Risikomanagement und Einsatzbedingungen für Systeme der künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) im Bankwesen veröffentlicht. Die neuen Bestimmungen enthalten insbesondere eine Reihe von Anforderungen, die die Kundenrechte direkt betreffen. Diese reichen von der Benachrichtigung der Kunden bei der Interaktion mit KI über die Erläuterung automatisierter Entscheidungen und die Möglichkeit der menschlichen Überprüfung bei Beschwerden bis hin zur strengen Kontrolle von Zahlungstransaktionen und Kreditentscheidungen durch KI. Thời báo Ngân hàng • 07/10/2026. Dieses Rundschreiben gilt für Kreditinstitute, Zweigstellen ausländischer Banken, Zahlungsdienstleister, Kreditauskunfteien, Anbieter mobiler Zahlungsdienste und diverse andere Einrichtungen des Bankensektors. Der Geltungsbereich der Regelung umfasst den Einsatz von KI im Bankwesen, bei Zahlungsdienstleistern, Kreditauskunfteien und mobilen Zahlungsdiensten. Ein von der vietnamesischen Staatsbank festgelegter Grundsatz besagt, dass KI menschliche Autorität und Verantwortung nicht ersetzt. Dienstleister bleiben rechtlich und gegenüber ihren Kunden für Entscheidungen verantwortlich, die von KI-Systemen getroffen werden. Organisationen ist es untersagt, sich auf die technischen Eigenschaften, die Autonomie des Systems oder die Verwendung von Produkten Dritter zu berufen, um ihre Haftung als Management oder rechtlich zu umgehen oder zu reduzieren. Dies ist bemerkenswert, da Banken KI zunehmend in den Bereichen Scoring, Beratung, Kundenservice, Betrugsprävention und Geschäftsprozessautomatisierung einsetzen. Laut Rundschreiben müssen KI-Systeme vor ihrer Implementierung nach ihrem Risikograd – hoch, mittel oder niedrig – klassifiziert werden. Insbesondere im Bankensektor können einige automatisierte Systeme, die elektronische Transaktionen durchführen oder automatisch Kreditentscheidungen vorschlagen, als risikoreich eingestuft werden.
